title: Democracies in glass houses
gist: Marcus Colla reviews Jan-Werner Müller's 'Street, Palace, Square', which argues political aesthetics reveal nothing inherent about political systems; 'transparency' is no democratic monopoly (fascist architect Terragni called his Casa del Fascio a 'glass house'), and visibility does not equal accountability. Physical space still shapes (facilitates, not determines) political conduct despite surveillance states and digital culture.

insights.claim: Visibility does not translate into comprehension or accountability, and transparency as an aesthetic is not exclusive to democracies, as fascist architect Giuseppe Terragni's Casa del Fascio claimed to be a 'glass house'.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla
insights.so_what: Caution against equating disclosure or transparency signalling with genuine accountability in institutions.
insights.quote: “Mussolinian concept that fascism is a glass house into which everyone can peer”

insights.claim: The aesthetic affinities of political systems reveal nothing inherent about them; beyond prestige projects, stereotypes about political aesthetics break down and space is always contested in any order.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla
insights.so_what: Symbolic signals are unreliable indicators of regime character.
insights.quote: Whatever the aesthetic affinities of specific political systems, they reveal nothing inherent about those systems.

insights.claim: Different urban forms facilitate, but do not determine, different kinds of political conduct, so whether a space is a building, square, boulevard or street matters.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla
insights.so_what: Urban design influences protest and civic dynamics relevant to political risk.
insights.quote: “Different urban forms”, he writes, “facilitate different kinds of political conduct”

insights.claim: Surveillance states and digital culture have reconfigured state-society relations but have not lessened the significance of physical space as a venue for political action.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla
insights.so_what: Physical mobilisation remains a key channel of political change despite digitisation.

insights.claim: John Quincy Adams claimed democracy is iconoclastic and 'has no monuments', but this overstated the case, as democratic capitals are packed with monuments.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla
insights.so_what: Historical context; limited direct investment relevance.
insights.quote: Democracy has no monuments. It strikes no medals.
